events.text: The clerks' copies of the Book of Fates come to your desk in bundles, each tied with a ribbon of the clerk's own colour. Your office is to hold every copy against the original, line by line, and to sign that they agree. Most years they do.

choices.text: Check every line, however long it takes

effects.log: You read until the lamps gutter. The copies agree. A young clerk, relieved, brings you tea you did not ask for.

choices.text: Sample one page in ten and sign

effects.log: You sign by the bell. Two of the ten are perfect, and you tell yourself the rest are perfect too.

events.text: A clerk has copied a whole season of harvest fates in the wrong hand: neat, round, and entirely correct. The Archive's rule says a wrong hand is a wrong copy. The clerk waits at your door, white to the ears.

choices.text: Pass the copy and note the hand

effects.log: You sign it. In the margin you write that the hand is not the rule and the fate is. The clerk bows until the ribbon falls off.

choices.text: Send it back to be copied again

effects.log: The rule is the rule. The clerk copies it all again overnight, in the correct hand, and the fates are the same.

events.text: In the audit of a clerk's copies you find a line that disagrees with the original: a widow's fate of hunger written as a fate of enough. The ink in the copy is a day fresher than the ink around it. Somebody inside the Archive has changed it.

choices.text: Report it to the Jade Secretariat

effects.log: The page goes up under seal. Minister Baek Ryeon sends back a note of thanks, and a question about who else saw it.

choices.text: Mend the line quietly and say nothing

effects.log: You write the true fate back in, in the clerk's own colour. The Archive is whole again, and you carry the secret of it.

choices.text: Sign the audit as it stands

effects.log: You sign. The widow will eat well this winter, and some other fate somewhere will pay for it.

events.text: A soul has appealed against the verdict of Judge Dobu's own bench, and the Ninth Hall must say whether the old judge erred. The soul in question is a ferryman who let a drowning stranger go under rather than risk the boat that fed twelve mouths.

choices.text: Uphold the verdict

effects.log: You read the case three times and find the old judge careful to the last line. The ferryman accepts it and asks only to be reborn near water.

choices.text: Lighten it, for the twelve mouths

effects.log: You lift a third of the weight from the verdict. Judge Dobu hears of it, nods once, and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Raise it, as a lesson to boatmen

effects.log: The Hall approves the sterner sentence. The ferryman does not argue, which is somehow the heaviest part.

events.text: An appeal against a magistrate of the Seventh Hall: a miller's soul, judged to a poor rebirth for short-weighting flour. The miller says the grain came short first and the weights followed the grain. The ledgers of the Seventh Hall do not mention the grain.

choices.text: Re-weigh the whole case, grain and all

effects.log: The grain was short, and so were three seasons of rain that nobody entered. The verdict is rewritten from the top.

choices.text: Forgive the miller and be done

effects.log: You strike the sentence. The Seventh Hall sends a polite complaint about precedent, which you frame.

choices.text: Let the first verdict stand

effects.log: The ledger says short-weight, and short-weight it stays. The miller bows to you with perfect courtesy.

events.text: A priestess's soul appeals against a verdict that she lied to her worshippers: she told them a god had spoken, and no god had. She says the village needed to hear it that year. The god in whose name she spoke has been asked, and answers that he was not listening.

choices.text: Judge only what she said

effects.log: The words were false, and you say so plainly. The sentence is small, and exact, and she thanks you for the exactness.

choices.text: Judge what the village gained

effects.log: You count the harvest saved, the feud ended. The verdict is gentle, and the god who was not listening is told to pay attention.

choices.text: Judge the god's name she used

effects.log: A false voice in a god's name is the gravest of lies. You say so, and the sentence is heavy.

events.text: A pair of brothers, souls both, appeal against the same verdict from opposite sides: one says it was too hard, the other that it was too soft, for the same dead farm and the same quarrel over a boundary stone. The stone itself has been brought to the Hall as evidence.

choices.text: Hear the stone, then the brothers

effects.log: It is an ordinary stone, moved a hand's breadth in the night by someone who is not in the room. You rule on that, and both brothers go quiet.

choices.text: Soften it for both

effects.log: You lighten both sentences by the same measure. The brothers leave still arguing about whose was lighter, and that, you think, is an improvement.

choices.text: Harden it for both

effects.log: You raise both by the same measure. The stone goes back to the boundary, and a priest of the Ninth Hall is sent to watch it.

events.text: You ride the four gates of heaven on the first night of the quarter, the South, the East, the West and the North, to see that each is shut and each gate-god is awake. At the East Gate a basket of tea-dumplings rides in under a lordly seal. The dumplings are full of mortal souls.

choices.text: Seal the basket and hold the carrier

effects.log: The carrier is a minor deity with a sly grin. The souls are sent on to proper judgment, and the Four Gates tell the tale for a month.

choices.text: Return the dumplings and file the report

effects.log: You return the basket, souls and all, to the nearest hall of judgment with a stamped report. It is the proper thing. It takes four hours.

events.text: The North Gate's god is asleep on his post, as he has been every winter for nine hundred years, and the gate has been shut anyway, by the cold. You stand in front of the sleeping god with the Warden's rod and no good instruction on what it is for.

choices.text: Wake him with the rod, gently

effects.log: He wakes, grumbles, and is awake for a full week, which the other three gates call a miracle.

choices.text: Let him sleep and mind the gate yourself

effects.log: You hold the North Gate through the night. At dawn he wakes, takes your hands in both his and calls you a better warden than the last nine.

events.text: A breach, in the dark hour at the West Gate: something small and clever has slipped through between the changing of the guard, and a ghost-lamp is moving along the wall toward the Inner Hall. The three other gates are watching to see how a new warden answers.

choices.text: Call the whole watch and run it down

effects.log: It is too fast for the watch. By the time the lamp reaches the Inner Hall it has gone out, and so has your sleep.

choices.text: Close all four gates and wait

effects.log: You bar all four gates until sunrise. The lamp is found in the morning in a clerk's desk. The clerk, you are told, was only curious.

events.text: A tide of souls arrives at the South Gate faster than the gate can count, and the count comes out two hundred short. Two hundred names are on the roll and not in the line. The gate-god swears none passed. The roll says otherwise, in your own hand.

choices.text: Sign the loss honestly

effects.log: You sign the report with the number it deserves. The Thunder Ministry will read it with interest, and you sleep badly and truthfully.

choices.text: Search the lower stairs yourself

effects.log: You find a hundred and ninety, asleep on the stairs like pilgrims. The last ten you never find.

events.text: You preside over the court's Great Session, the three days each year when the ministers of the Jade Secretariat and the Thunder Ministry sit face to face under one roof. This year they come quietly, which is worse. The first motion on the roll is yours to table or to take up.

choices.text: Take it up, and let them argue it out

effects.log: They argue for a day and a half and agree on something small. The Chancellor's chair has never been so quiet, and so well respected.

choices.text: Table it and turn to the harvest rolls

effects.log: The motion is shelved without a vote. Minister Baek Ryeon bows with relief; Marshal Cheon Mu does not.

events.text: Marshal Cheon Mu of the Thunder Ministry rises in the Great Session to ask that the Southern Gate be doubled, and Minister Baek Ryeon rises in answer to ask that it be halved. The hall turns toward the Chancellor's chair like a field of sunflowers.

choices.text: Split the gate's watch between them

effects.log: It is half a victory for each and a full one for you. The Ministries whisper that the Chancellor is wise, which they have never said of anyone.

choices.text: Ask them both what the gate is for

effects.log: The hall goes silent. Neither Minister has an answer ready, and you let the silence stand until they find it.

events.text: Seol Haneul, an old friend and an older clerk, is brought before the Great Session on a minor charge that is plainly someone's grudge. The record is yours to read aloud. It is thin as paper, and every minister in the hall is looking at his own sleeves.

choices.text: Read it in full, and let it speak for itself

effects.log: It speaks. The charge falls before you finish, and Seol Haneul, who has never wept in heaven, blots his eyes on an inkwell.

choices.text: Dismiss the charge from the chair

effects.log: You use the Chancellor's authority and the hall bows to it. It is the first time you have felt how large that authority is, and how little of it you want.

events.text: The Great Session opens badly. A rumour has run the corridors that the Chancellor's seal was used last month on a decree the Chancellor never signed. The Jade Secretariat demands an inquiry, and the Thunder Ministry demands it be held now, in this hall, with the doors shut.

choices.text: Accept the inquiry in open session

effects.log: You sit through it from the chair itself. The decree was forged by a copyist, and the copyist, who is terrified, is dismissed with a warning instead of a sentence.

choices.text: Defer it a month and hold the Session

effects.log: You hold the Session and the inquiry waits. The Ministries are displeased for different reasons, which, you remind yourself, is how you know it was balanced.

events.text: The Great Session breaks down. A vote on the winter fates ends in shouting, and for a long moment the Jade Secretariat and the Thunder Ministry stand on opposite sides of the hall with their sleeves up. The Chancellor's gavel is in your hand. It is only a gavel.

choices.text: Adjourn and speak to each Minister alone

effects.log: By evening each is asking whether the other is angry with them. The Session resumes in the morning, and finishes in an hour.

choices.text: Call the hall to order, loudly

effects.log: The hall comes to order, resentfully. The vote is taken, and half the court does not forgive it until spring.

events.text: The Keeper of the Fate Archive before you takes the Archive's key off her neck and puts it round yours. It is a small, plain key. She says it opens a single door, and that the door is the one nobody ever asks to see.

choices.text: Ask what is behind it

effects.log: "Every fate that was changed," she says, "and who changed it. Read it once and then forget the way." You will not forget the way.

choices.text: Thank her and go to your new desk

effects.log: The Archive is quieter than the clerks' hall, and the shelves are taller. You hang the key where you can feel it.

events.text: Seol Haneul stands in the doorway of the Archive with a jar of cloud-wine and a very official face. "The Keeper of the Fate Archive," he announces, to nobody, and then bursts out laughing. The clerks down the hall start clapping before they know what it is for.

choices.text: Celebrate with him first

effects.log: He pours himself a small cup and you a large tea, and spills half of both. For one evening the oldest records in heaven are kept by two people who are laughing too hard to read.

choices.text: Ask him to keep it down

effects.log: He doesn't, and you don't really want him to. The Keeper's first order is lost in the noise.

events.text: The Ninth Hall is smaller than a magistrate's hall has any right to be, and it is the one where the hardest appeals end. The outgoing magistrate hands you the gavel and says that the Hall has one rule, which is that the Hall is never in a hurry.

choices.text: Promise to take as long as it takes

effects.log: The old magistrate nods and leaves, lighter than she came. The Hall settles around you like a heavy coat.

choices.text: Ask whether she ever regretted a verdict

effects.log: "Every one," she says, "and I would give every one again." It is the most useful answer you could have been given.

events.text: Judge Dobu comes to the Ninth Hall on your first morning, very old, with a stool of his own because he does not trust the Hall's. He sits at the back and says nothing for the whole hearing. When the Hall rises, he says only: "Good. You were slow."

choices.text: Thank him for the stool

effects.log: He says it is a good stool. It is, you realise, the best compliment he knows.

choices.text: Ask him to sit closer next time

effects.log: He says he will, and does not, and comes to every hearing for a year.

events.text: The Warden's rod is carved from the wood of a tree that grew at none of the four gates but is said to have watched all of them. The outgoing Warden presses it into your hands and tells you that the four gate-gods will test you in the first month, one by one, in ways they will deny.

choices.text: Thank them in advance, all four

effects.log: You send a gift to each gate-god. The East Gate keeps its dumplings; the North Gate stays awake for a whole afternoon.

choices.text: Carry the rod and say nothing

effects.log: The tests come. The rod is quiet, and so are you. By spring all four gods admit that you passed.

events.text: The four gates of heaven give you the four words they answer to, one each, whispered at dawn by their gate-gods. The South Gate's is a name, the East's a song, the West's a number, and the North's a long and comfortable silence. You are told never to write them down.

choices.text: Learn them by heart, one gate at a time

effects.log: It takes you a month. By the end you could open any gate in heaven in your sleep, and sometimes, in a way, you do.

choices.text: Ask whose names they were

effects.log: The South Gate's name belonged to the first gatekeeper. The others the gates will not tell, and you do not press.

events.text: The Chancellor's chair is cut from a single piece of cloud-jade and set so that every minister in the Great Hall must look up to speak to it. The old Chancellor steps down from it with relief and says, "It looks high. It isn't. Everyone sits at your feet and watches your hands."

choices.text: Sit in it, and look at the ministers

effects.log: They watch your hands. You keep them still, and open, and no one in the Hall mistakes the gesture.

choices.text: Ask the old Chancellor to stay one session

effects.log: The old Chancellor stays, sits at your elbow, and corrects nothing. It is, you realise, a greater kindness than advice.

events.text: Minister Baek Ryeon and Marshal Cheon Mu come to your investiture together, in robes of their ministries, standing at opposite ends of the Hall. They bow to you at the same moment, perfectly, and do not look at each other. The whole court sees it. The whole court understands who is holding the middle.

choices.text: Bow back to each, equally

effects.log: You bow to the minister and the marshal, and heaven decides to take the bow as a promise.

choices.text: Bow to the Jade Throne instead

effects.log: The Throne, which has never answered anyone, seems this once to approve.
